title: Minimum Tariff Valuation Framework
summary: This thread tracks the government's periodic setting of minimum tariff values for imported goods to prevent under-invoicing. Over time, the mechanism evolved from simple price setting to a more structured approach that mandates the use of historical minimum values when new notifications are repealed, while maintaining the primacy of the Customs Valuation Rules 2000.

evolution.legal_basis: Transitioned from simple administrative orders to a structured framework integrating repealed notification values into current valuation rules.
evolution.procedure: Shifted from fixed price lists to a hybrid model where minimum values act as a floor, with flexibility for higher valuation based on brand/origin.

timeline.change: Initial establishment of minimum value conditions for motor vehicles.
Expansion of minimum values to consumer goods and specific vehicle types.
Periodic update of tariff values for various goods.
Refinement of tariff value tables and categories.
Introduction of 'provisional' determination of minimum values.
Formalization of the rule that repealed minimum values must be considered in current valuations.
Reiteration of valuation rules and historical price consideration.
Continued application of minimum valuation thresholds and valuation rules.

Customs Act 1969: The Government is empowered by section 25(3) of this Act to set minimum valuation criteria for specific imported goods.
First Schedule: This instrument establishes minimum valuation conditions for new motor vehicles and automobiles classified under specific headings of this schedule.
Customs Duty: The collection of this duty on new motor vehicles and automobiles is subject to the minimum valuation requirements established by this order.
Manufacturer’s Price Certificate: Importers are required to submit a valid price certificate from the vehicle manufacturer to determine the minimum value for customs purposes.

In cases where the manufacturer's certificate is unavailable, a certificate from a marketing company with at least thirty percent ownership by the manufacturer may be accepted upon submission of proof of such ownership to the Customs Commissioner.
Certificates issued by agents or dealers appointed by the manufacturer are explicitly excluded from being accepted for valuation purposes.

The value derived from this certificate serves as the minimum threshold for customs valuation, unless the declared transaction value of the vehicle is higher, in which case the higher declared value prevails.

Customs Act 1969: The Government issued this S.R.O. under the authority granted by Section 25(3) of the Customs Act 1969 to determine the minimum value for customs duty assessment on specific motor vehicles.
The Act defines the framework within which the First Schedule is maintained and under which the Government may prescribe valuation criteria for imported goods.
S.R.O. 190-AIN/2010: This previous customs notification is explicitly repealed by the current S.R.O.
First Schedule: The First Schedule of the Customs Act 1969 identifies the specific H.S. Codes under Heading Numbers 87.03 and 87.04 that are subject to the new vehicle valuation requirements established by this order.
Customs Duty: This order establishes the criteria for determining the minimum value used to assess customs duty on the import of new motor cars, double cabin pick-ups, and other motor vehicles.
Manufacturer’s Price Certificate: Importers are mandatorily required to submit an invoice issued directly by the manufacturer during customs clearance.
Price certificates or invoices issued by dealers or agents of the manufacturer are explicitly declared unacceptable for the purpose of establishing minimum value.
Value: The declared value in the manufacturer's invoice serves as the minimum value for assessment purposes, provided that higher values found in recognized international price guides or official manufacturer price lists take precedence if they exceed the invoice price.

(২) “Renowned brand” অর্থ খ্যাতনামা বা বহুল প্রচলিত বা বিখ্যাত ব্র্যান্ড।

Customs Act 1969: Section 25(3) of this Act empowers the Government to issue notifications regarding tariff and minimum values of goods.
The current order utilizes the legal authority granted under the Act to amend a previously issued S.R.O.
S.R.O. 165-AIN/2016: This notification is formally amended to revise tariff and minimum value criteria for various categories of goods.
Specific terminology within the original notification is replaced with new definitions to provide clarification on valuation standards.
TABLE-1: This table provides the tariff values in US dollars per unit for specific imported commodities, including tea, sugar, and petroleum products.
The values listed serve as a basis for assessment as part of the formal amendment to the existing tariff order.
TABLE-2: This table outlines the minimum values in US dollars per unit for a wide range of goods such as food preparations, personal care items, plastics, and electronics.
The minimum value is established to reflect the standard transaction price for general quality goods, while allowing for higher valuation for premium products.
Imported Goods: The order defines and updates the valuation framework for various imported goods by categorizing them into tables based on their tariff or minimum value.
Valuation criteria distinguish between general brands and renowned brands, with specific conditions applied based on the country of origin or technical specifications.
Value: The order introduces an explanatory note defining minimum value as the transaction value for general quality imported goods, while acknowledging that superior quality goods should naturally command a higher price.
Brand classification between Renowned and General is explicitly defined to assist in the consistent application of these values.
